name: LeFort 1 maxillary advancement

card.summary: Upper-jaw surgery that cuts and moves the maxilla forward for midface projection; a standard orthognathic operation whose cosmetic claims rest mostly on bite and cleft research.
card.aka: Le Fort I osteotomy, maxillary advancement, LeFort
card.note: Major surgery under general anaesthesia; relapse, numbness and bite or joint problems are documented, and stability varies with the direction of movement.

quick.overview:
A Le Fort I osteotomy is a horizontal cut through the upper jaw, made from inside the mouth, that lets the surgeon move the maxilla forward, back, up or down and fix it with plates. In clinical practice it is used for bite problems, a recessed or vertically long upper jaw, cleft-related underdevelopment and, together with lower-jaw surgery, for sleep apnoea.

Looksmaxxing forums discuss it as a way to project the midface, support the area under the eyes and correct underbites, often paired with a lower-jaw operation. Published studies document stability and outcomes in functional and cleft patients; there is little research on cosmetic-only advancement.
quick.mechanism: The bone cut passes above the tooth roots and below the cheekbone and eye socket, freeing the tooth-bearing maxilla so it can be repositioned in three dimensions. Plates and screws hold the new position while bone heals; orthodontics aligns the teeth around the operation.
quick.risks: Documented concerns include bleeding, swelling, infection, nerve numbness, relapse of the new position (greater for some movement directions and large advancements), nasal and lip changes and a months-long recovery. It is regulated as routine surgery and performed by oral and maxillofacial or craniofacial surgeons.

lead: Le Fort I osteotomy is an upper-jaw operation in which the maxilla is cut horizontally above the roots of the teeth, mobilised and fixed in a new position, usually through an incision inside the mouth.[1][3] It is the most common maxillary procedure in orthognathic surgery and can advance, set back, shorten, lengthen or expand the upper jaw.[2] In looksmaxxing circles it is known as LeFort 1 or maxilla advancement and is discussed as a method of increasing midface projection.[17]

Clinical research on the operation comes mainly from bite-correction and cleft lip and palate patients. Reviews and studies report that its stability depends on the direction of movement, the fixation method and the technique, and that cleft patients often need maxillary advancement because earlier repair surgery can restrict maxillary growth.[7][8] Studies of purely cosmetic advancement are limited.

Forum discussions on looksmax.org describe advancement distances of several millimetres, counter-clockwise rotation, effects on lip seal and under-eye support, and combination with lower-jaw surgery; these are reported experiences rather than trial findings.[17][18][19]
infobox: Horizontal, above tooth-root tips and below the infraorbital foramen, through the maxillary sinuses (as described on forums)[18]
Advancement, setback, impaction, downgraft, rotation, expansion
Maxillary deficiency or excess, bite problems, cleft-related hypoplasia, sleep apnoea

paras: In Le Fort I surgery the upper jaw is separated from the rest of the midface along a horizontal line, which allows the tooth-bearing segment to be moved in three dimensions and then fixed with plates and screws.[1][3] It is used for deficiencies in the front-to-back dimension, for vertical excess of the maxilla (long-face pattern), and for transverse problems, sometimes with the maxilla split into segments.[1][3]

A review dedicated to the technique covers its indications, contraindications, preoperative assessment, surgical technique and complications, and stresses close collaboration between surgeon and orthodontist and a sound grasp of facial analysis.[3] Most reviews treat Le Fort I as one component of a larger plan that may include a mandibular osteotomy, a chin procedure and orthodontics.

A frequently cited review of orthognathic stability reported that the predictability of surgical movements varies mainly with the direction of movement, then fixation type and surgical technique; superior repositioning of the maxilla was described as the most stable movement.[7]

General encyclopedia summaries report that surgery usually produces a stable bite, improved chewing and high patient satisfaction, and that advancing the maxilla by a few millimetres changes lip position by a smaller amount, so soft-tissue changes are often subtle.[2] Those figures come from an AI-generated overview and vary across the original studies.

Diminished maxillary growth is a recognised consequence of cleft repair, and many patients with cleft lip and palate undergo Le Fort I advancement; a retrospective cohort study examined how often the procedure was needed after repair.[8] Reviews of cleft orthognathic surgery describe maxillary advancement, often with mandibular setback and other procedures, as altering profile and chewing and setting the stage for later lip and nasal revision.[5]

In cleft patients with large deficiencies, advancement of more than 10 mm may be required, and distraction osteogenesis has been proposed as an alternative to conventional osteotomy for very large movements.[6][9][10] A randomised trial compared the five-year stability of cleft maxillary distraction with orthognathic surgery,[11] and another randomised trial examined rigid fixation after distraction.[12]

Human studies of Le Fort I surgery include a randomised trial comparing cleft maxillary distraction with orthognathic surgery over five years,[11] a randomised trial of fixation after distraction,[12] a clinical trial of soft-tissue response and facial symmetry using three-dimensional photogrammetry after orthognathic surgery,[13] and a trial examining relapse after orthodontic therapy combined with surgery in skeletal Class III patients.[14]

A systematic review and meta-analysis of maxillomandibular advancement for obstructive sleep apnoea, which involves a Le Fort I plus a mandibular osteotomy, pooled 627 adult patients from 22 populations to estimate efficacy and safety.[4] Registered trials include comparisons of two designs of patient-specific plates for Le Fort I fixation and of nasolabial changes with different alar base sutures after Le Fort I.[15][16] No published trial has been identified that tests Le Fort I advancement solely for cosmetic midface projection.

General descriptions of orthognathic surgery list bleeding, swelling, infection, nausea and nerve-related numbness as the main immediate risks, with some movements such as maxillary impaction carrying higher risk.[1] Long-term concerns reported in cleft and Class III patients include skeletal relapse, which is a focus of the cleft distraction and relapse studies above.[9][11][14]
Initial healing is described as taking two to six weeks and complete bone healing a further two to four months.[1]

On looksmax.org, Le Fort I is discussed as a way to move the upper jaw forward and fix underbites, often alongside a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy and genioplasty, with members debating how much advancement looks natural.[17][18][19] One user compiled a guide stating that advancement is typically in the range of 4 to 10 mm and describing options such as widening and rotation.[18] Another member reported 8 mm advancement and 5 mm impaction with a lower-jaw operation covered by insurance because of a severe underbite, and noted that 8 mm did not look as large as expected.[19]

timeline.event: Simon P. Hullihen publishes one of the first known jaw-correction cases.[1]

Hugo Obwegeser, with Trauner, is credited with the lower-jaw sagittal split osteotomy; he is also credited with popularising the Le Fort I osteotomy, according to an AI-generated encyclopedia overview.[2]
Rigid titanium plate fixation reduces long jaw immobilisation.[2]
A hierarchy-of-stability review ranks maxillary superior repositioning as the most stable orthognathic movement.[7]
A systematic review and meta-analysis assesses maxillomandibular advancement for sleep apnoea.[4]

lore.intro: Forum threads treat Le Fort I as a core hard-tissue procedure for midface projection and underbite correction, usually part of a multi-surgery plan.[17][18][19]

claims.claim: Advancing the upper jaw also improves under-eye support and the infraorbital area.
claims.believers: A member asks whether Le Fort I improves under-eye support and gets the reply that moving the upper jaw would help slightly.[17]
claims.experts: Published studies in the sources examine soft-tissue changes and symmetry after orthognathic surgery, but none specifically measures infraorbital support after Le Fort I.[13]

claims.claim: Maxilla advancement of roughly 4 to 10 mm is the usual goal.
claims.believers: A forum guide states the maxilla is usually advanced in that range, and a poster reports having 8 mm advancement and 5 mm impaction.[18][19]
claims.experts: Reviews of cleft surgery note that some patients need more than 10 mm of advancement, and stability varies with the direction and amount of movement.[6][7]

claims.claim: Le Fort I with a lower-jaw operation can be covered by insurance for an underbite.
claims.believers: A forum poster reports that jaw surgery for a severe underbite was covered by insurance.[19]
claims.experts: Clinical sources describe bite correction as a functional indication for orthognathic surgery; coverage depends on the insurer and country and is not addressed in the reviewed literature.[1]

claims.claim: Surgical movements are stable once healed.
claims.believers: Forum guides present advancement as a fixed outcome of the operation.[18]
claims.experts: A review of the stability hierarchy reports that stability differs by movement direction, and studies of cleft and Class III patients examine relapse after surgery.[7][11][14]
